The Spanish DPA issued a fine of €1800 against an online clothes store for processing personal data without data subjects' consent, for failing to have a privacy policy, and for the use of non-essential cookies without providing appropriate information through a cookie banner.

The French DPA issued a fine of €1,500,000 against a software solutions provider acting as a processor for medical analysis laboratories, due to a data breach concerning the data of almost 500,000 data subjects in violation of Articles 28, 29, and 32 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined an adult content website €8000 for its unlawful use of cookies and providing insufficient information related to their nature and purposes, as well for having an outdated privacy policy, which was based on data protection laws prior to the entry into force of the GDPR.

The Austrian DPA held that the operator of a search engine must delete a link to a database which contains the home address of the data subject if the latter fears for his physical integrity after receiving a death threat.

The Romanian DPA issued a €500 fine against a neighborhood owners association for failing to cooperate with the DPA by not providing requested information related to an investigation regarding video surveillance recordings, in violation of Article 83(5)(e) GDPR.

The Dutch DPA investigated the Fraude Signalering Voorziening (FSV), a fraud-signalling application used by the Tax and Customs Administration until February 2020. It found that the Minister of Finance, as controller, processed personal data in FSV from 4 November 2013 to 27 February 2020 without a legal basis, without a specified purpose, with inaccurate data and with excessive retention. It also found inadequate security (access, logging and log checks) and that the data protection officer was not involved properly or in time in the DPIA. The AP imposed six separate administrative fines totalling EUR 3,700,000, raising the base amounts for the nature, gravity and duration of the breaches, negligence, the data categories and, for some, earlier relevant infringements.

During an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software, the Garante checked a hospital in Perugia and its provider ISWEB. It found the hospital processed personal data via the whistleblowing application without a specific privacy notice, without recording it in the register of processing, without a DPIA, and without adequate security (navigation logs kept on firewalls, credentials of a departed RPCT still active). It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 13, 14, 25, 30, 32 and 35 GDPR and fined the hospital EUR 40,000. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended and the hospital had cooperated.

During an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software, the Garante examined ISWEB S.p.A., which supplies a whistleblowing platform to clients including the Perugia hospital and acts as their processor. ISWEB used a hosting provider (Seeweb) without a proper Article 28 arrangement, both for its own processing as controller and for processing done for clients as processor, including without the hospital's prior authorisation. ISWEB argued the breaches were merely formal and that the IP addresses involved were not personal data, but the Garante rejected this. It found the Article 28 infringements, fined ISWEB EUR 40,000, ordered it to bring the processing into compliance within 30 days and report back, and ordered publication of the decision.

A commercial agent complained that the company cut off her work email account without notice, kept it alive, and ignored her requests for access to her data. The company also failed to answer the Garante's information requests, so the Garante used the Guardia di Finanza to serve them. The Garante found breaches of fairness and storage limitation, of the duty to inform, of the access right and response deadlines, and of the duty to answer the authority. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered access for the complainant, deactivation of the account with automatic notices, a ban on further processing of the extracted data and better procedures, and fined the company EUR 50,000.

A individual complained that Made in Italy s.r.l.s. called him twice for promotion without consent and ignored his access, erasure and objection requests. The company also never answered the Garante's request for information and did not defend itself. The Garante found breaches of Articles 15, 17, 21, 6 and 7 GDPR and of the Code (Art. 130(3), 157). It issued a warning, ordered the company to answer the complainant, banned further processing of his data, and fined it EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.

A debtor complained that the bank Findomestic contacted his wife, who was guarantor on only one of his loans, about another loan for which he alone was liable. The bank explained that a staff member mistakenly entered the wife's phone number as a contact, so two SMS messages about payment status were sent to her in October 2020. The Garante found the processing unlawful and in breach of the principles of lawfulness, fairness, transparency and data minimisation. It fined the bank EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A man who had bought goods from the company asked it on 10 July 2020 for access to his personal data and related information under Article 15 GDPR, and the company did not answer within the legal time limit. During the procedure the company only listed categories of data, called the request unfounded and pretextual, and argued the data were already known to him and belonged to his firm. The Garante rejected these arguments, since the request concerned his own personal data, and found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15. It ordered the company to reply to the data subject within 30 days and fined it EUR 10,000.

The Garante received a report that the café 'Caffè Antica Roma', run by Rebirth s.r.l., had a non-compliant video surveillance system. The company ignored two requests for information, so the Guardia di Finanza inspected and found 14 working cameras with no information signs and no labour inspectorate authorisation or union agreement. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Articles 114 and 157 of the Code, and fined the company EUR 15,000, also ordering publication of the decision.

After a report about a video surveillance system at the company's premises, the Guardia di finanza inspected in November 2021 and found 15 working cameras. Signage was missing in several areas, two cameras exceeded those authorised by the labour authority (authorisation was requested only in 2018 for a 2013 installation), and the three people with access to the footage shared credentials and only one had been instructed. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 13, 29 and 32 GDPR and Article 114 of the Code, rejected the argument that employee consent cured the problem, and fined the company EUR 10,000. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

The municipality of Orte was fined €20,000 by the Italian DPA for operating photo-traps without adopting any compliance measures, for failing to provide information to the data subjects, and for failing to provide direct contact to their DPO.

The Danish DPA proposed that Danske Bank should be fined €1,345,000 for lack of storage and erasure procedures in over 400 systems containing the personal data of millions of data subjects. The police will investigate the case before a final decision is made in the courts.

Following press reports, the Belgian DPA investigated the use of thermal cameras and a second-line health check at Brussels Airport to screen passengers for COVID-19 in 2020. The Litigation Chamber found that the airport company and its contractor (the first-aid company running the second-line check) lacked a valid legal basis for the processing of health data, and that the airport company breached transparency duties and the data protection impact assessment rules. It fined the airport company EUR 200,000 and the contractor EUR 20,000, and reprimanded the airport company for finalising its impact assessment late. The decision was later partly annulled (first defendant) and wholly annulled (second defendant) by the Market Court.

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber examined the use of thermal cameras by Charleroi airport to check passengers' temperature during COVID-19. It found there was no adequate legal basis for processing health data, and that transparency and information duties were breached. The DPIA was carried out three months after the processing began and was inadequate. It imposed a EUR 100,000 fine and a reprimand for shortcomings in the processing register. The decision was later partly annulled by the Market Court.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, thermal cameras at Brussels Airport (Zaventem) screened passengers for a temperature above 38°C. Ambuce Rescue Team then carried out a second check, a symptom questionnaire. The Litigation Chamber found that the airports had no valid legal basis for processing this health data, and it also found shortcomings in the information given to travellers and in the impact assessments. It fined Ambuce Rescue Team EUR 20,000, alongside fines of EUR 200,000 on Zaventem and EUR 100,000 on Charleroi. A note on the page says the Market Court later annulled the decision entirely as regards Ambuce Rescue Team.

A customer complained that Piraeus Bank kept sending account-movement alerts (Winbank Alerts) for her debit card to an e-mail address belonging to a third person with the same name, and did not fix it after being told. The bank said the joint account holder had registered an address differing only by a dot, which Gmail treats as identical, and that no breach occurred. The Authority found the bank breached confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(f)) and its duties to notify the breach to the Authority and the data subject (Arts. 33 and 34). It fined the bank EUR 10,000 in total and issued a warning to put in place technical and organisational measures to verify e-mail addresses given for alerts.

A head of department at a municipality complained that the former mayor, now a municipal councillor, sent letters containing her personal data to many recipients, including trade unions, after she chose to be appraised by the new mayor. The former mayor argued that he acted under public authority (Art. 6(1)(e)) and for legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)). The Authority found that sending the letters to the municipal employees' union and to the national federation of municipal employees (POE-OTA) breached the lawfulness principle of Art. 5(1)(a) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 on him as controller.

A former managing director and employee complained against his ex-employer, which had restored and analysed the mailboxes from his work laptop after dismissal and refused his requests for erasure, restriction and objection. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of lawfulness and minimisation (Art. 5(1)(a), 6(1)(f)), information duties, data subject rights (Arts 15, 17, 18, 21) and Art. 28. It ordered compliance with the complainant's requests, introduction of a policy charter and an end to processing data older than 5 years, and imposed a fine of EUR 7,500. The Market Court later partially annulled the decision.

The Italian DPA ordered a news company to cease any further publication on the contents of messages between a school director and a student which were allegedly involved in a love affair, considering that the dignity and confidentiality of the persons involved outweighed the company's journalistic freedom to report on those details.

Following an Article 60 GDPR cooperation procedure, the Swedish DPA issued a reprimand against a newspaper subscription service which violated Articles 6(1), 12(3) and 21(2) GDPR by failing to stop sending marketing emails despite the data subject's objection.

The Danish DPA held that an access request by a data subject asking his previous employer to provide all emails, notes and letters sent or signed by him was excessive according to Article 12(5)(b) GDPR, since it comprised a very large amount of personal data predominantly connected to his duties and not personal attributes.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Swedish DPA determined that the controller violated Article 32(1) GDPR by failing to provide an appropriate level of security for the internal handling of customers' accounts.

The Hungarian DPA imposed a fine of approximately €1,300 on a car repair shop. The DPA held that the shop violated Articles 5, 6 and 13 GDPR by failing to properly inform its employees about CCTV surveillance and for using it in areas intended for work breaks.

IMY examined the privacy information that Klarna Bank AB gave customers on its website in spring 2020 (17 March to 26 June 2020). It found that the information was incomplete, misleading or missing on purposes and legal basis for the 'Min Ekonomi' service, recipients such as credit reference agencies, transfers to third countries, retention periods, data subject rights and automated credit decisions. IMY held that Klarna breached Articles 5(1)(a), 5(2), 12(1), 13 and 14 GDPR. It imposed a single joint administrative fine of SEK 7,500,000, treating the information as one and the same processing. Klarna's improvements to the information during the review were counted as mitigating.

The Swedish DPA conducted an investigation and issued a fine of approximately €730,000 against Klarna Bank for not providing data subjects with adequate information related to their processing activities, in violation of various provisions under Articles 5, 12,13 and 14 GDPR.

"Comparables" can be considered personal data and therefore a legal basis is required to process or provide this information to third parties Article 6(1)(f) The Disputes Chamber proceeds to dismiss claim: The Disputes Chamber finds that the complaint does not concern any processing of personal data concerning the complainant or affecting the complainant according to the specific criteria developed by the Disputes Chamber.

The Municipality of Genoa's local police used a fines-management platform (ScatWeb) supplied by Brav s.r.l., which acted as processor. Unauthorised people accessed it because officers' first-access passwords (their badge numbers) were never changed and the access URL was circulated. The Garante found that Brav had not ensured password quality or forced a change at first login, left the service available over insecure http, and lacked server logs with IP addresses for the breach period. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR and fined Brav EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measure was imposed on the Municipality.

The Italian DPA fined Uber a total of €4,240,000 for violations relating to 1,500,000 data subjects in Italy, including lack of transparency and consent and failure to notify the DPA of a personal data breach.

The Finnish DPA issued a reprimand against the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for the late notification of a data breach to both the DPA and the data subjects under Articles 33 and 34 GDPR. The DPA held that although controllers can investigate potential data breaches before the 72-hour time limit in Article 33 GDPR starts running, the Ministry failed to do so after it had concluded its investigation, without providing justified reasons for the delay.
The Belgian DPA held that a municipality was entitled to send emails to data subjects who had previously registered their email addresses for a campaign as volunteers.
The Danish DPA reprimanded a municipality for sharing unnecessary and sensitive personal data about an employee with over 50 of her coworkers in violation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.
The Swedish DPA reprimanded a controller for violating Article 12(3) GDPR by not informing a data subject about a delay of their erasure request within a month of receiving it.

The Finnish DPA found the social and health authority of a city to have breached Article 6(1) GDPR and Article 10 GDPR by requesting data subjects to provide it with personal data that it had no legal basis for processing.

The Belgian DPA reprimanded a controller for failing to delete a former client's personal data in violation of Article 17(1) GDPR, and for not handling the erasure request within the one-month period under Article 12(3) GDPR.

The Danish DPA issued a warning against a company related to its intended use of a facial recognition system. The DPA held that the company may only process biometric data in this way with the data subjects' consent under Article 9(2)(a) GDPR.

The Norwegian DPA fined a company €9,775 for unlawfully enabling automatic forwarding of an employee's emails in violation of Article 6(1)(f), for lack of information as per Article 13, failure to assess their objection as per Article 21, and required them to improve internals controls for employee emails as per Article 24 GDPR.

The Irish DPC announced a decision fining Meta Platforms Ireland Limited EUR 17 million. The decision followed an inquiry into twelve data breach notifications received in 2018. The DPC found that Meta failed to have appropriate technical and organisational measures in place to be able to readily demonstrate the security measures it applied to protect EU users' data. The decision was adopted through the Article 60 co-decision process, with objections from two authorities resolved by consensus.

The Irish DPC ran an own-volition inquiry into Bank of Ireland after a series of personal data breach notifications about inaccurate data uploaded to the Central Credit Register. It found the bank infringed Articles 33 (late or imprecise notification to the DPC), 34 (late communication to affected customers) and 32 (inadequate technical and organisational measures). The DPC issued a reprimand, ordered the bank to implement a procedure and confirm compliance within 90 days, and imposed several fines totalling EUR 463,000.

The Icelandic DPA reprimanded a primary school for mistakenly including the medical data of a student in emails sent to the parents of other students when handling a bullying case, in violation of Articles 9, 5(1)(f), 24, 25 and 32 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA held that, under the GDPR, direct marketing via email may not require the data subject's consent. However, it is still necessary to inform the data subject pursuant to Article 14 GDPR at the latest at the time of initial contact.

The Belgian DPA held that a car dealership violated Articles 12 and 15 GDPR by not complying with an access request, as well as Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 24 and 32 GDPR due to a lack security measures which led to a data breach.
The Romanian DPA issued a fine of approximately €2000 against a real estate agency for not granting a data subject's access request in violation of Article 15 GDPR.

The Tuscany Centre local health authority notified the Garante of two data breaches: a medical record copy handed to the wrong person, and two radiology reports mailed to each other's patients by mistake. The Garante joined the two proceedings and found that health data were disclosed to third parties without a legal basis, in breach of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 9 and 32 GDPR. Because the conduct had exhausted its effects and corrective measures were already in place, it imposed no corrective orders. It fined the authority EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee of a regional environmental agency complained that the agency published in full, without anonymisation and indexed by search engines, a resolution approving a union conciliation settlement. It also referred to a criminal case in which he was acquitted. The Garante found that the agency had no legal basis for disseminating the data online, including data on criminal proceedings, and that this breached Articles 5, 6 and 10 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-octies of the Code. It fined the agency EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

A complainant had earlier asked a shipyard company to erase his data and got no answer; in decision n. 166 of 29 April 2021 the Garante fined it and ordered it to reply to him within 60 days. The company neither complied nor answered the Garante's information request, so the Guardia di finanza inspected it in October 2021, and only then did the company write to the complainant. The Garante found a breach of the duty to comply with a corrective order (Art. 83(6) GDPR) and of Art. 157 of the Italian Code (failure to answer information requests). It imposed a single fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision. A note says the court appeal was later extinguished.

The UK DPA fined law firm €116,784.27 (GBP 98,000) for contravening Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR by "failing to process personal data in a manner that ensured appropriate security of the personal data.”

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Estonian DPA issued a warning to a controller. Among other things, the data subject was not able to create a user account without consenting to direct marketing in violation of Article 7(2) GDPR.

The Greek DPA issued a fine of €2000 against a private school because its director constantly attended and monitored an employee's online courses without adequately informing her of the legal basis to do so, and despite her objection, in violation of Articles 5(1)(a), 5(2) and 13 GDPR.

This is a press release announcing two fines, totalling HRK 1.6 million. Only the second one matches this Fino entry. A retail chain notified the Agency of a personal data breach: employees had filmed the video surveillance monitor with their mobile phones, and the footage spread on social media and in the media. The Agency found that the chain had taken some organisational steps, such as training, internal rules and confidentiality statements, but not adequate technical and organisational measures, either before or after the incident. It also did not regularly test the effectiveness of its measures. The Agency imposed an administrative fine of HRK 675,000 for breaching Article 32 GDPR.

A complainant objected that Harpa, buying tickets through the Tix online ticketing system, required his national identification number (kennitala) or date of birth. Persónuvernd found this collection was not necessary to fulfil the contract, since tickets could be delivered using other identifiers, and that customers were not told registration was optional. Harpa breached the lawfulness, data minimisation and transparency principles, the legal basis rules and the national ID number provision. It was ordered to stop collecting and to delete the data already collected, and fined ISK 1,000,000. The fine was reduced because Harpa could not change its practice once Covid rules required registration and it acted in good faith, but increased somewhat by its poor cooperation.

The Icelandic DPA reprimanded a university for not providing students adequate information regarding the processing of their personal data when remotely monitoring exams taken at home via Zoom due to the COVID19 pandemic, in violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.

The Basque DPA held that Articles 6(1)(c) and 6(1)(e) GDPR supplied a legal basis for a local police force to include personal data in files sent to the Chief of the Police, the Mayor’s Office, and the Councilman of Citizen Security. It is still assessing whether this practice complies with the principle of data minimisation.

The UK DPA issued a €23,850 (GBP 20,000) fine against Royal Mail for sending unsolicited direct marketing emails in violation of provision 22 of the UK Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003.

The Danish DPA held that a controller violated Article 32(1) GDPR for not carrying out sufficient tests which could have revealed the security issue which led to a personal data breach on their platform.

The Danish DPA held that a controller had not adopted appropriate technical and organisational measures pursuant to Article 32(1) GDPR, which led to a personal data breach caused by an employee's error.

In September 2020 attackers gained unauthorised access to the email accounts of a number of members of parliament and staff of the Norwegian Parliament, and data including bank details, national ID numbers and health data may have been exposed from 13 accounts. Datatilsynet found that Parliament had not implemented suitable technical and organisational measures, in particular two-factor authentication, even though its own risk analysis from March 2020 had identified the lack of it as high risk. It rejected Parliament's arguments about the pandemic and the lack of instruction authority over MPs and party staff. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 2,000,000 under Articles 32(1)(b) and (d) and 5(1)(f). The decision could be appealed by 15 August 2022.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the DPA of Malta reprimanded a controller pursuant of Article 58(2)(b) GDPR) for requiring an ID-photo as identification method to exercise an access request. The DPA also ordered the controller to comply with the request pursuant of Article 58(2)(d) GDPR.

Bremen's DPA issued a €1,900,000 fine against Brebau GmbH (a residential property management company) for unlawfully processing the sensitive data of over 9500 prospective tenants, including aspects like their skin colour, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, health status, hairstyle and body odour.

The Danish DPA found that the Høje-Taastrup Municipality violated Article 32(1) GDPR because it did not have guidelines or objective criteria in place to assess which users have access to a database containing personal data.

A subscriber asked a telecom provider to remove their name, address and phone number from its public online directory, but a technical error and an administrative mistake meant the data stayed online for years. The provider could not show that the subscriber had consented to publication, and it wrongly logged the phone requests as complaints. The authority found violations of Articles 17(1)(b), 5(2), 6(1) and 12(2) GDPR and fined the provider HUF 5,000,000. The erasure request itself was rejected as moot because the data had been deleted during the proceedings.

The Hungarian DPA fined an organisation and its Chair approximately €8,000 each for failing to inform the signatories of a campaign about the processing of their personal data and several other GDPR violations.

The Hungarian DPA issued a fine of €13,000 against an online directory operated by a telecom operator (including customers' names, addresses and mobile numbers) for breaching the accountability principle and processing data without a valid legal basis, in violation of Articles 5(2) and 6(1) GDPR.

The Austrian DPA (DSB) held that a controller unlawfully relied on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and Article 6(1)(c) GDPR as legal bases for processing of personal data obtained from GPS-tracking devices installed on company vehicles used by its employees.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the DPA of Malta reprimanded a controller (Article 58(2)(b) GDPR) for requesting the data subject to sign an agreement in order to process his erasure request. The controller also had to reply to the request (Article 58(2)(d) GDPR).

The Norwegian DPA intends to fine a company €29,376 for monitoring and accessing a prior employee's emails without a legal basis in Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, for lack of information as per Article 13, failure to assess their objection as per Article 21, and lack of technical and organisational measures as per Article 24.

The Dutch DPA investigated how the Minister of Foreign Affairs handles Schengen visa applications in the NVIS system. It found that the security plan was missing, physical protection was insufficient, access rights, logging and incident procedures were incomplete, and applicants were not adequately told who receives their data. It fined the Minister EUR 565,000 for breaching Articles 32(1) and 13(1)(e) GDPR. It also imposed penalty-payment orders to end the continuing violations, with deadlines of 24 October 2022 (security) and 24 March 2022 (information). The press release adds that by May 2023 the information duty was met in time, while the security measures came late and a EUR 50,000 penalty payment was due.
The Italian DPA held that the Bank of Italy violated Articles 5 and 6 GDPR by unlawfully disclosing personal information in the context of a recruitment procedure.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Estonian DPA handled three complaints regarding the same controller. The DPA reprimanded the controller for not adequately responding to data subject's requests. The authority also held that requesting an ID for verification purposes is acceptable when there is reasonable doubt about the data subject's identity (Article 12(6) GDPR).

The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) held that the Capital Region of Denmark violated Article 32(1) GDPR for negligence related to its health platform's software updates, which led to two separate data breaches involving 4,459 data subjects' health data.

A driver involved in a traffic accident in the Heraklion port asked the port authority for access to its CCTV footage of the accident. The authority refused, citing an ongoing GDPR compliance process, and ignored two follow-up requests. Before the HDPA it claimed the footage had already been deleted after 6 days, but the HDPA found the footage was still held when the first request was made. The HDPA found a breach of the right of access (Art. 15(1) with Art. 12(1),(2) GDPR) and fined the port authority EUR 30,000.
The Austrian DPA found that the Minister of Finances implementing instructions from a a parliamentary anti corruption committee falls within the scope of the GDPR.

The UK DPA issued a €60,000 (GBP 50,000) fine against a loan broker for making unsolicited direct marketing text messages in violation of provision 22 of the UK Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003.
The Hungarian DPA imposed a fine of approximately €25,000 on a debt management company which, among others, violated Article 12(1) GDPR by failing to accept a verbal request for erasure.
The French DPA held that a French online respondent violated Chapter V of the GDPR by using Google Analytics, which led to unlawful transfers of personal data to Google LLC in the U.S.

A former executive of Costampress S.p.A. complained that after he was dismissed the company kept his work email account, did not give him back his company phone number which had also been used privately, and blocked and examined his company laptop, including private WhatsApp chats. The Garante found the company's processing unlawful for breaching the fairness principle and the transparency and information duties (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12 and 13 GDPR). Other alleged breaches (Arts. 5(1)(c), 6 and 20) were dropped. It fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Italian Garante investigated Clearview AI, a US facial recognition company that scrapes images from the web and builds biometric data, after press reports, complaints and reports from privacy groups. It rejected the company's argument that the GDPR does not apply and found breaches of the processing principles, legal basis, special-category rules, transparency, access rights and the duty to appoint an EU representative. It banned further collection and processing of data of people in Italy, ordered deletion of that data, ordered appointment of a representative, and fined the company EUR 20 million, the maximum under Art. 83(5). The Art. 22 allegation was not upheld.
The Italian DPA issued a fine of €3500 against a local health authority for disclosing a medical report to the wrong patient in violation of Articles 9 and 5(1)(f) GDPR.

Scanshare S.r.l., processor for the Regione Toscana's public recruitment competition, uploaded candidates' results to a web server without access authentication. A link sent by mistake to a candidate matched the upload folder, so data of about 3,600 candidates became accessible and was shared in a WhatsApp group. The Garante found that Scanshare had not applied adequate security measures (Art. 32) and had used a hosting provider (Hostinger) without the controller's prior written authorisation (Art. 28(2)). It fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A complainant, listed years earlier in an online directory of shiatsu operators, repeatedly asked for his data to be deleted but received no answer. The Garante found that the company publishing the portal was the controller and was responsible for the failure to erase and to reply, even though the site was run by its majority shareholder who no longer had access. The company also did not answer the Garante's request for information, but no separate fine was imposed for that. The site was taken offline only after the Garante intervened, so no corrective order was needed, and a fine of EUR 5,000 was imposed with publication of the decision.

A property owner complained that a real estate agency kept phoning him with promotions and ignored his access and erasure request sent by certified email. The agency had taken his number from public websites and a Google search, without consent or another legal basis, and had not given him the Article 14 information. It also answered the Garante's information requests late and inadequately. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, restricted the processing of web-sourced data without consent, ordered procedures for handling data subject rights and for giving information, and fined the company EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision.

The Authority opened an ex officio procedure against Budapest Bank over its AI-based analysis of recorded customer service calls, which assessed the emotional state of callers and employees and ranked calls for call-backs and quality control. It found breaches of the principles of purpose limitation and lawfulness, legal basis, transparency, the right to object, accountability and data protection by design and default. The bank was ordered to bring the practice into line, stop analysing emotions and guarantee data subject rights, including adequate information to employees. A fine of HUF 250,000,000 was imposed, taking into account the bank's turnover of HUF 81 billion and the seriousness and long duration of the infringement.
The UK DPA (ICO) fined Tempcover Ltd £85,000 for sending almost 30,000,000 unsolicited direct marketing messages in violation of Regulation 22 PECR.

The Austrian DPA held that a law firm had a legal basis for presenting a data subject's personal data as evidence in court proceedings under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR as the legitimate interest in doing so outweighed the data subject's interest in keeping his personal data confidential.
The Danish DPA expressed criticism on TV 2 for processing sensitive data without a legal basis regarding sexual misconduct allegations against an employee during in an internal investigation.

The Norwegian DPA fined a municipality €29,880 for publishing a confidential document with a pupil's sensitive personal data, including potential diagnoses such as ADHD, in breach of Articles 32(1)(b), 6, and 5 GDPR.

The municipality published a document on its public mail journal website in which 10 of 21 attachments contained confidential special-category data about a pupil, because the attachments were not marked as exempt. A journalist noticed it and four different IP addresses accessed the document. The Datatilsynet found a lack of appropriate security measures (no routines for follow-up checks of published documents) and publication without a legal basis. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 300,000 after lowering the culpability from grossly negligent to negligent following the municipality's reply.

The Finnish DPA held that a parking services provider violated Article 5(1)(c) and Article 25 GDPR because, in cases where a technical failure occurred with the payment machine, data subjects were prompted to provide their phone number to receive the receipt via SMS, and were not adequately informed that they could also opt for a printed copy without having to provide their phone number.
The Romanian DPA fined a news website approximately €1000 after it published video recordings of medical patients in breach of Articles 6 and 9 GDPR.

The Norwegian DPA intends to fine a private investigation company €5,000 for unlawfully credit rating the former boyfriend of a client and for not adhering to the accountability principle as per Article 5(2) GDPR, cf. Article 24, and also requires them to implement internal controls for their credit rating process.

The Danish DPA rejected the data subject’s complaint and erasure request because it found that the controller’s legitimate interest to retain the personal data, outweighed the interests of the data subject.
The UK DPA (ICO) fined Home2sense €240,317.08 (GBP 200,000) for making unsolicited direct marketing calls in violation of Regulation 21 and 24 PECR.
The German Federal DPA issued a decision specifying which data a telecommunications and internet company should provide to a data subject when handling an access request under Article 15 GDPR.

A data subject complained that TSM gave an incomplete reply to his access, erasure and objection requests after he received contract forms in its name for a professional training course. TSM only said it had deleted his data, gave no information on the processing, did not confirm the objection, and ignored two requests for information from the Garante. The forms also carried no privacy notice. The Garante found breaches of Articles 13, 15 and 21 GDPR and of Articles 157 and 166(2) of the Code, issued a warning, ordered TSM to answer the complainant, banned further processing of his data and fined TSM EUR 40,000. A note at the top says the appeal ended with a final judgment favourable to the company by the Tribunal of Rome in January 2023.

The Italian DPA ordered Google to de-list search results which associated a data subject’s name to a public job competition’s selection process, taking the storage limitation principle under Article 5(1)(e) GDPR into consideration.

IMY opened an investigation after the Uppsala regional board reported a personal data incident. The board had sent Excel files with patient data, including health data and personal identity numbers, by internal email. Only the transport was encrypted, not the file contents, and this went against the region's own guidelines. IMY found a breach of Article 32(1) GDPR for the period 25 May 2018 to 7 May 2019 and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 300,000.

After the Uppsala region reported a personal data incident, IMY examined how Akademiska sjukhuset emailed patient data to patients and referring hospitals abroad. Health data was sent by email that was not reliably encrypted, because the hospital relied on opportunistic TLS, and medical records were also stored in Outlook. This went against the region's own guidelines. IMY found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) between 25 May 2018 and 7 May 2019 and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 1,600,000 on the hospital board.

A small Irish credit union accidentally left member enquiry reports in a directors' area of its website that became searchable online for about a week in November 2018, exposing data of 76 members, 34 of them children. It notified the breach, and the DPC opened an own-volition inquiry. The DPC found infringements of the security obligations (Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)), and also of Articles 24, 28 and 30(1). It issued a reprimand and a single fine of EUR 5,000, calculated on the Article 5(1)(f) infringement, noting the credit union's prompt reaction and cooperation but also its negligence.
The DPA rejected complaint of the data subject who had stated that his rights were violated because data controller sent compensation via postal service.

The Irish DPC found no personal data breach pursuant to Article 32 GDPR when the Personal Injuries Assessment Board (PIAB) unexpectedly received an unencrypted USB storage device in a ripped envelope by ordinary post.
The Belgian DPA issued a reprimand against a website owner for violating Article 12 and Article 13 GDPR and ordered them to comply with their processing register.

The Estonian DPA held that the legal basis for transferring a data subject's debt data to a third party was legitimate interest, not contractual necessity. The DPA also reprimanded the controller for failing to reply to an access request within one month.

The Polish DPA imposed on Fortum Marketing Sales Polska S.A. as a controller and on PIKA Spółka z o.o. as its processor administrative fines of about €1,000,000 and €53,000 respectively for the breach of data confidentiality and the lack of sufficient security measures.
The Polish DPA imposed a fine of approximately €120,000 on a bank for failing to notify data subjects of a personal data breach, in violation of Article 34(1) GDPR.
The UK DPA (ICO) fined Energy Suite £2000 for making unsolicited direct marketing calls in violation of Regulation 21 PECR.

The Slovenian DPA held that a company could have informed its employees about their proximity with COVID-19 high-risk contacts within its workplace, without disclosing the full name of the infected employees, in violation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA carried out an investigation in response to a claim against Grindr by a human rights NGO, and found no violations of GDPR as to consent regarding processing of personal data for advertisement purposes or the processing of special categories of personal data.

Under Article 60 GDPR the Belgian DPA (LSA) and other concerned authorities ordered a controller to comply with a data subject's request to erasure according to Article 58(2)(c) GDPR, because it did not comply with the request.

In April 2020 the Maltese Commissioner learned of a security incident at C-Planet (IT Solutions) Ltd and opened an investigation. He found that the company processed personal and special-category data unlawfully and failed to apply appropriate security measures. It also failed to notify the breach to the authority in time and to inform the affected data subjects. He imposed a fine of EUR 65,000 and ordered erasure of the unlawfully processed data. The company cooperated fully.

The Dutch DPA received complaints that DPG Media Magazines (formerly Sanoma Media Netherlands) demanded a copy of an identity document before handling access or erasure requests made outside the secure login environment. DPG's policy always required the copy, did not offer the option of a redacted copy for digital requests, and left requests unhandled if no copy was supplied. The AP found this created unnecessary barriers and breached Article 12(2) GDPR. It imposed the base fine of EUR 525,000 under its category III fine policy, without increase or reduction. DPG stopped asking for ID copies on 17 December 2020 and uses a verification email instead.

A news report says the Austrian data protection authority imposed a fine of eight million euros on the REWE group over its 'jö Bonus Club' loyalty programme, citing GDPR violations. The decision is not final and REWE International AG says it will take legal action, denying responsibility for the data processing of the separate company jö. It is the second fine of this kind, after a EUR 2 million fine against the jö Bonus Club in summer 2021. The article does not describe the specific infringements or the reasoning.

The Norwegian DPA fine the Parliament about €196,400 (NOK 2,000,000) for a data breach where perpetrators got access to employees' email accounts and health-related data, enabled by the lack of two-factor authentication and organizational measures.

The Garante received a report that the privacy notices published by the Frosinone local health authority named consent as the legal basis for processing patients' data for care purposes. Its investigation found further defects: missing or wrong legal bases, missing retention periods, a reference to legitimate interest and to data portability. The authority corrected the notices after the investigation began. The Garante declared the processing unlawful for breach of transparency and information duties (Arts 5(1)(a), 12, 13 GDPR), imposed no corrective measures because the conduct had ended, and fined the authority EUR 7,500 with publication of the decision.

A worker complained that the occupational health company appointed by his employer gave an irrelevant reply to his access request for his personal data and ignored a second request. The company only sent a copy of the health file in March 2021, after the Garante intervened. The Garante found breaches of the right of access and the deadline rules (Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR) and fined the company EUR 4,000, ordering publication of the decision.

A press report revealed vulnerabilities in the Covid-19 screening platform and the 'Smart4You' app used by the Marche regional health authority: sequentially generated QR codes and a tax-code decoding function allowed third parties to see names, phone numbers and, in one case, a swab result. The authority notified a breach, and the Garante opened proceedings. It found breaches of integrity and confidentiality, security of processing and the duty to carry out a data protection impact assessment, plus Article 75 of the Italian Code. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended and remedies were adopted, but a fine of EUR 14,000 was imposed and the decision was ordered to be published.

The Greek DPA ordered the Ministry of National Defense to reissue a military status certificate with only the data subject's name on it because the previous one violated the principle of data minimisation by mentioning more than the name.

The Finnish DPA held that a social services entity violated Article 6(1) and Article 10 GDPR by requiring potential foster parents to provide criminal record certificates following the wrong national law procedure specifically established for this purpose.

The UK DPA served the Ministry of Justice an Enforcement Notice to bring its processing into compliance by responding to data subjects' pending access requests and carrying out organisational changes to ensure that future ones are dealt with in the time frame provided for by Article 15 GDPR.

The European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) issued a reprimand against the European Parliament for illegally transferring data to the US for having unclear cookies banners and therefore placing cookies without valid consent, having a data protection notice that did not comply with its transparency requirements, and failing to answer an access request by the complainants.
